newsitem.title: FINLAND: FINNISH 1998-99 SPEND PLAN ENCOURAGING - ANALYSTS.
newsitem.headline: FINNISH 1998-99 SPEND PLAN ENCOURAGING - ANALYSTS.

text.p: The Finnish government's decision on Tuesday to cap state budget expenditure in 1998-99 at this year's level was in line with expectations and would have little impact on financial markets, analysts said.
They nevertheless applauded the resolve of the government to not become blinded by healthy growth figures and embark on new spending to attract unhappy voters on the left.
"The Lipponen government looks determined to keep its very good track record intact," said Risto Murto, chief economist at Erik Selin Finance.

He and other analysts said Tuesday's budget decisions would not affect Finnish bonds as the five-party coalition had simply taken one more step on the path it staked out on taking office in April 1995, and reaffirmed in February last year.
"Fiscal policy is no problem ... the broad outlines of the savings policy were agreed already earlier," said chief economist Petteri Hirvonen at brokerage Davy Protos.

Esko Torsti, head of market advisory at SE-Banken, said that a marginal part of the strengthening seen in benchmark bonds on Tuesday could perhaps be attributed to news of the cabinet's continued austere fiscal policy stance.
"It amounted to a blessing over this government to stay united behind its savings decisions," he said. "This had been expected, but it was good news nonetheless," he added.
Analysts said it was a good sign that the government had resisted the temptation to use growing tax revenue to finance new spending schemes.

Supporters and backbenchers of the coalition's two left-wing parties have repeatedly and loudly criticised the tight fiscal stance, and both the Social Democratic Party of Prime Minister Paavo Lipponen and the junior Leftist Alliance fared badly in municipal elections last October.

The government said it had agreed on spending ceilings for the two remaining annual budgets of its term in office to 1999. It capped 1998 budget expenditure at 191 billion markka and set a 192 billion markka ceiling for 1999, it said in a statement.
Total spending in the 1997 state budget approved by parliament is 190.3 billion markka.
The deficit of the state finances would be 20 billion markka in 1998, down from some 28 billion this year, Finance Minister Sauli Niinisto told reporters.
Denis Strandell, head of treasury at Aktia Bank, said the decision had been "undramatic but fundamentally encouraging."
"It confirms that we will stick with the same fiscal policy as before," he said.
The long end yield gap over German Bunds was unlikely to narrow from current levels at slightly over 30 basis points on the back of the budget news, the analysts said.
It was more likely that the differential would remain steady. And the gap could widen if EMU jitters intensified or if strong growth in Finland led to fears of quicker inflation, they said.
